items.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...people like Nat Hentoff and a group of people were talking about... [INTERVIEWEE] It’s always an issue because it’s an issue socially.

ctx.x: enough to say, come on, I can show you. And they were some of the first ones. You know you would go into some of those after-hours places and you’ll see all kinds of people, white, black people, just enjoying the music. And you’d start seeing guys play together. And on the bandstand, look, I’m going to hire this person because I like what they can do, they should be heard. You know what I mean? So the music, to me, through my studying would be inside the forefront of a lot of it. And I think it still should be.

Is there any — a number of years ago a Jazz Times came out and the cover of it said “Race Matters.” And it was a coverage of a symposium they had had. And people like Nat Hentoff and a group of people were talking about, I guess, does race matter in jazz now? Now that was a few years ago, but I wonder, is there any racial disharmony or is it even an issue anymore?

It’s always an issue because it’s an issue socially. So it’s always something that has to be worked on. It’s always something that should be thought about and not just in terms of black and white. You know there’s other issues that are coming across now because there’s always so much — the shakedown of the devil, he’s 24/7. He will never give up. So he’s always stirring up something. And we see it from time to time with the plight of Jewish people having to go through or the Muslims or somebody else moves in the…
